title: Currencies: RBA cuts US dollar reserves in sign of hedge against Trump
full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia has become the first major central bank to confirm that it has reduced its US dollar holdings as part of a wider trend by policymakers to diversify their assets away from the United States under an unpredictable White House.
Data from the International Monetary Fund and think tank surveys showed for the first time this year that central banks are planning to trim their exposure to the greenback, rather than build up reserves over the next decade to hedge against political risk and swings in currencies and bonds.
The RBA indicated in its 2025 annual report that less than half of its currency reserves were in US dollars, which is the lowest level since 2012, according to a Deutsche Bank report to clients.
"The central bank has discreetly reduced the target share of US dollars to 45 per cent from 55 per cent, and shifted that allocation to euros," said Lachlan Dynan, a macro strategist at Deutsche Bank.
"This is the first G10 central bank to have effectively confirmed some reduction in its target US dollar allocation in recent years, even if the allocation remains within the range of historical allocations."
The euro now accounts for 30 per cent of Australia's foreign currency reserve, while the yen, Canadian dollar, yuan, pound and South Korean won make up 5 per cent each. The RBA's assistant governor for financial markets, Christopher Kent, said at a fireside chat in August that the central bank was a "little long" the US dollar when he was questioned about the reduction in holdings, but noted the change was not a forecast about the currency.
"It wasn't really based on some deep insight because I don't have any deep insights on exchange rates, other than don't predict where they're going," he told Reuters. "We hold currencies that we deem to be highly liquid ... We hold these for policy purposes in case we ever decide there's a need to intervene."
The tinkering with the RBA's asset base comes amid a global debate over the greenback's role as the world's main reserve currency, driven by unpredictable policies from the White House and rising geopolitical risks in the Middle East and Europe.
Even so, no clear alternative has emerged, with the US dollar eking out a 1.2 per cent gain this year against a basket of currencies, driven by the Federal Reserve's elevated interest rates - which are expected to climb higher in the months ahead - and the highly liquid American bond market.
Less prominent currencies are, however, quietly gaining ground. A survey by the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum showed central banks have been buying more Australian dollars, Canadian dollars and Norwegian krone.
But the biggest winner from the so-called "dedollarisation" has been gold, which hit a record high above $US5500 an ounce at the start of the year as the precious metal became the focus of central bank reserve management strategies, the survey showed.
These moves match the broader market's growing concern about US debt that cracked $US40 trillion ($56 trillion) in August, which was also among the worst months for US Treasuries. Yields on 30-year bonds climbed to a two-decade high of 5.3 per cent as investors demanded higher returns for holding American debt.
"I haven't seen any data or reporting for other central banks, but what we do know on the whole, at least in Asia, is that there is a deep antipathy and caution toward the US dollar exposure," said Richard Franulovich, head of foreign exchange strategy at Westpac.
As economies and businesses deal more in other currencies, central banks are expected to gradually adjust their reserves to match real-world trade in a crisis.
In Australia, for example, mining giants BHP and Rio Tinto already settle some of their commodity contracts in Chinese yuan, Franulovich pointed out.
While the US dollar is likely to retain a prominent role because of the size of its economy and trading volume, foreign exchange strategists said its dominance is expected to erode over time as trade patterns shift and political risks grow.
"Between the geopolitical fragmentation, the multipolarity of the world, [and] lingering question marks about the integrity and stability of US institutions, central banks will rebalance their foreign reserves," Franulovich said. "It will happen slowly, but it will happen."
